Bright Morning Star
brīt môr´nĭng stär
n. / title (Christ's last self-designation in Scripture; rendering Greek ho aster ho lampros ho proinos)
The morning star is the planet Venus, the last light to rise before dawn and the sign that the night is nearly over. The image is fixed in Balaam's oracle of a Star out of Jacob.

Biblical Definition

The last self-designation the Lord gives in Scripture: “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). He promises the same to the overcomer at Thyatira: “and I will give him the morning star” (Rev 2:28). The image runs back to Balaam — “there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel” (Num 24:17) — and forward through Peter: “ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts” (2Pe 1:19). Malachi's parallel is the sunrise: “the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (Mal 4:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines morning star as the planet Venus, when it precedes the sun in rising; and day-star as the morning star, Lucifer, Venus, the star which precedes the morning light.

MORNING-STAR, n. The planet Venus, when it precedes the sun in rising.

DAY-STAR, n. The morning star; the star which precedes the morning light.

Key Scripture

Rev 22:16 — "I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star."

Rev 2:28 — "And I will give him the morning star."

Num 24:17 — "I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth."

2Pe 1:19 — "We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:"

Mal 4:2 — "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall."

Modern Corruption

The title is confused with Lucifer's, and Isaiah's morning star is a fallen king while Revelation's is the Lord Himself.

expand to see more

The objection is old and is still circulated: Isaiah 14:12 addresses one whom the Latin rendered Lucifer, son of the morning, and Revelation 22:16 has Christ call Himself the bright and morning star; therefore, it is said, the two are the same figure. They are not the same word and not the same claim. Isaiah's oracle is a taunt against the king of Babylon — the passage names him in verse 4 — whose pride said, I will ascend into heaven, and whose fall is the point; the epithet is a description of a brief brightness that was extinguished, and the Latin translators' choice of Lucifer, light-bearer, is a translation, not a name. The morning star of Revelation rises and does not set.

The pastoral force of the title is in its timing, and it is easy to miss. The morning star is not the dawn; it is the last light of the night and the promise that the dawn is coming. Peter puts the Christian in exactly that hour: a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn and the day star arise in your hearts. The church lives in the interval, with a sure word of prophecy and no daylight yet, and the title is given to a people who are being told to hold on.

The last line of the Bible's last self-designation places two things side by side: the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. He is David's origin and David's descendant at once, which is the paradox the Lord had already put to the Pharisees from Psalm 110 — if David call him Lord, how is he his son? A title that holds both ends of that is not a decoration on the end of the book; it is the summary of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aster (G792), star; lampros (G2986), bright; proinos (G4407), of the morning; phosphoros (G5459), day star, light-bringer; Hebrew kokab (H3556), star.

expand to see more

Greek ho aster ho lampros ho proinos (G792, G2986, G4407) — the bright and morning star; Revelation 22:16, and Revelation 2:28.

Greek phosphoros (G5459) — day star, light-bringer; 2 Peter 1:19 only.

Hebrew kokab (H3556) — star; Numbers 24:17; and helel (H1966), Isaiah 14:12, of the king of Babylon.

Usage

"“I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” — the last self-designation in Scripture."

"“Until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts” — the church's hour is before dawn."

"“There shall come a Star out of Jacob” — Balaam's oracle, spoken for hire and true."
